title: Index
body:
The position of an element in an [[Array]], counting from **0**. An array of size *n* has
indices `0` through `n-1`, and `a[n]` is off the end.

```c++
const int SIZE = 10;
int num[SIZE];
for (int i = 0; i < SIZE; i++)    // '<', not '<='
	num[i] = 0;
```

`i <= SIZE` is the off-by-one that reads one past the array, and because **C++ does not check
bounds** it usually does not crash. It reads whatever memory is there, which turns a
[[Runtime Errors|runtime error]] into a [[Logic Errors|logic error]] you cannot see.

The index is also the loop's [[Control variable]], which is why array work and
[[Repetition]] are the same topic in practice. `i % size` wraps an index back into range;
see [[Division Algorithm]].

Under the hood `a[i]` is `*(a + i)`, address arithmetic scaled by the element size, which is
why [[Dynamic Arrays]] can be subscripted through a bare [[Pointer]].
